questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: identify the null hypothesis in a test
questions.stem: A researcher tests whether a new drug reduces blood pressure. What is the null hypothesis?

options.text: The drug has no effect on blood pressure

options.misconception: confuses the research hypothesis with the null hypothesis
confuses the null with the alternative

options.text: The sample size is too small
options.misconception: confuses a design issue with a hypothesis

questions.explanation: The null hypothesis states that there is no effect, so the drug does not change blood pressure. The research hypothesis is that it reduces blood pressure, and the other options describe design concerns or the alternative, so each distractor names a real concept applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: What does the null hypothesis always claim?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: interpret the mean of a dataset
questions.stem: What does the mean of a numeric dataset represent?

options.text: The middle value when data is sorted
options.misconception: confuses mean with median

options.text: The sum of all values divided by the count

options.misconception: confuses mean with mode

options.text: The spread of values around the center
options.misconception: confuses central tendency with dispersion

questions.explanation: The mean is the arithmetic average, computed by summing all values and dividing by the number of observations. The median, mode, and standard deviation describe other properties of the distribution, so distractors map to related but distinct measures.
questions.hint: Which measure adds every value and divides by how many there are?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard deviation of a small sample
questions.stem: Compute the sample standard deviation of the values 2, 4, 6, 8. Round to two decimals.
questions.explanation: The mean is 5, squared deviations are 9,1,1,9 summing to 20, divided by n-1=3 gives 6.67, whose square root is 2.58. This uses the sample formula with n-1 in the denominator.
questions.hint: Use n-1 in the denominator for a sample.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A p-value of 0.03 in a hypothesis test means:

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
options.misconception: confuses p-value with probability of null being true

options.text: If the null were true, the observed result would occur 3% of the time

options.misconception: confuses p-value with statistical power
confuses significance with effect magnitude

questions.explanation: A p-value measures how surprising the observed data would be if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, not power, and not a measure of effect size, so each distractor reflects a common misreading.
questions.hint: What is assumed true when computing a p-value?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A significance level of 0.05 means:

options.text: We reject the null 5% of the time when it is actually true
We fail to reject the null 5% of the time when it is false
options.misconception: confuses type I error with type II error

options.text: The probability the alternative is true is 95%
options.misconception: confuses significance level with posterior probability
confuses alpha with effect size threshold

questions.explanation: Alpha is the probability of a type I error, rejecting a true null hypothesis. It is not the type II error rate, not a posterior probability, and not an effect size cutoff, so each distractor applies a real quantity to the wrong concept.
questions.hint: Alpha controls which error?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of data falls within one standard deviation of the mean?

options.misconception: confuses one standard deviation with the median split
confuses one with two standard deviations
confuses one with three standard deviations

questions.explanation: The empirical rule says about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution. The other options are the percentages for zero, two, and three standard deviations respectively.
questions.hint: Recall the 68-95-99.7 rule.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: In a linear regression of y on x, a slope of 2 means:

options.text: y increases by 2 units for each one-unit increase in x
x increases by 2 units for each one-unit increase in y
options.misconception: reverses the predictor and response roles

options.text: The correlation between x and y is 2
options.misconception: confuses slope with correlation coefficient
confuses slope with intercept

questions.explanation: The slope quantifies the change in the response variable per unit change in the predictor. Reversing roles, equating slope with correlation, or conflating it with the intercept are common misinterpretations.
questions.hint: Which variable changes in response to the other?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute a simple linear regression prediction
questions.stem: A fitted line has intercept 3 and slope 4. Predict y when x = 5.
questions.explanation: Using y = intercept + slope * x gives 3 + 4*5 = 23. This applies the fitted linear equation directly.
questions.hint: Plug x into y = a + b x.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: select an appropriate chart for categorical data
questions.stem: Which chart type is best for comparing counts across distinct categories?

options.misconception: confuses trend over time with category comparison
confuses binned numeric distribution with categories
confuses relationship between two numerics with category counts

questions.explanation: A bar chart represents values for discrete categories with separated bars. Line charts show trends, histograms show numeric distributions, and scatter plots show relationships between two numeric variables.
questions.hint: Which chart uses separated bars for distinct groups?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: How does a histogram differ from a bar chart?

options.text: A histogram bins a continuous numeric variable; a bar chart compares categories
A histogram always uses color; a bar chart does not
options.misconception: confuses aesthetics with structural difference

options.text: A bar chart requires a legend; a histogram does not
options.misconception: confuses presentation with definition
misses the continuous-versus-categorical distinction

questions.explanation: A histogram partitions a continuous numeric range into bins and shows frequencies, while a bar chart displays values for discrete categories. Color and legends are stylistic, not definitional.
questions.hint: What kind of variable does each chart summarize?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Which measure of center is least affected by extreme outliers?

options.misconception: mean is sensitive to outliers
mode can be unstable or absent
range is a measure of spread, not center

questions.explanation: The median depends only on the middle position, so extreme values do not change it much. The mean is pulled by outliers, the mode may be ambiguous, and the range measures spread rather than center.
questions.hint: Which measure uses only the middle position?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute the median of an even-count dataset
questions.stem: Find the median of 3, 7, 1, 9. Round to two decimals.
questions.explanation: Sorted values are 1,3,7,9; with an even count the median is the average of the two middle values, (3+7)/2 = 5. This handles the even-count case correctly.
questions.hint: Average the two middle values when the count is even.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A type I error in hypothesis testing is:

options.text: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
options.misconception: describes type II error
describes a correct decision

options.text: Failing to reject a true null hypothesis
options.misconception: describes a correct decision

questions.explanation: A type I error is a false positive: rejecting the null when it is actually true. The distractors cover the complementary type II error and the two correct decisions, completing the decision matrix.
questions.hint: Which cell of the decision table is a false positive?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A type II error in hypothesis testing is:

options.misconception: describes type I error

options.text: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis

options.misconception: describes a correct decision

options.text: Failing to reject a true null hypothesis
options.misconception: describes a correct decision

questions.explanation: A type II error is a false negative: failing to reject the null when it is actually false. The distractors cover type I error and the two correct decisions, completing the decision matrix.
questions.hint: Which cell of the decision table is a false negative?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: An R-squared of 0.8 in a regression model means:

options.text: 80% of the variance in the response is explained by the predictor
The correlation between x and y is 0.8
options.misconception: confuses R-squared with correlation magnitude
confuses explained variance with prediction accuracy
confuses R-squared with slope

questions.explanation: R-squared measures the proportion of variance in the response explained by the model. It is not the correlation, not the fraction of exact predictions, and not the slope, so each distractor misattributes a real coefficient to R-squared.
questions.hint: What does R-squared measure in terms of variance?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A model that performs well on training data but poorly on new data is likely:

options.misconception: underfitting gives poor performance on both sets
confuses good training fit with calibration
confuses low bias with good generalization

questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise in the training data and fails to generalize. Underfitting harms both sets, while calibration and bias are separate concepts.
questions.hint: Which failure mode memorizes training noise?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A value is 14, the mean is 10, and the standard deviation is 2. Compute the z-score.
questions.explanation: The z-score is (value - mean) / standard deviation = (14-10)/2 = 2. This standardizes the value relative to the distribution.
questions.hint: Subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A correlation coefficient of -0.9 between two variables indicates:

options.misconception: confuses magnitude with strength sign
ignores the negative sign
confuses near-zero with near-minus-one

questions.explanation: The sign indicates direction and the magnitude indicates strength; -0.9 is strong and negative. The distractors misread the sign or magnitude.
questions.hint: Consider both sign and magnitude.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: recognize correlation does not imply causation
questions.stem: Two variables are strongly correlated. What can we conclude?

options.misconception: confuses correlation with causation

options.text: There is an association, but causation is not established

options.misconception: confuses correlation with linearity proof
confuses correlation with independence

questions.explanation: Correlation indicates association, not causation; confounding or reverse causation may explain it. It also does not prove linearity or imply independence.
questions.hint: What does correlation alone not establish?

questions.stem: Which chart best shows how a value changes over time?

options.misconception: confuses part-to-whole with trend
confuses relationship with ordered trend
confuses distribution summary with time trend

questions.explanation: A line chart connects ordered observations over time, making trends visible. Pie charts show parts of a whole, scatter plots show variable relationships, and box plots summarize distributions.
questions.hint: Which chart connects points in chronological order?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A pie chart is a poor choice when:

options.text: Showing many categories with similar sizes

options.misconception: two categories are fine for a pie chart
that is exactly what pie charts do

options.text: Showing a single snapshot in time
options.misconception: pie charts suit single snapshots

questions.explanation: Pie charts become hard to read with many similar slices. Two categories, percentages summing to 100, and a single snapshot are all appropriate uses, so those distractors describe valid cases.
questions.hint: When do slices become hard to compare?

questions.stem: Multicollinearity in multiple regression occurs when:

options.text: Predictors are highly correlated with each other
The response is uncorrelated with predictors
options.misconception: describes low explanatory power, not multicollinearity
confuses multicollinearity with residual non-normality
confuses multicollinearity with intercept value

questions.explanation: Multicollinearity means predictors are strongly correlated among themselves, inflating coefficient variance. The other options describe unrelated regression issues.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A researcher specifically tests whether a new process increases yield (not just changes it). Which test is appropriate?

options.misconception: two-tailed tests any difference, not a directed one
confuses categorical association with mean comparison
confuses group comparison with a directed mean test

questions.explanation: When the alternative hypothesis is directional, a one-tailed test is appropriate. A two-tailed test checks for any difference, chi-square tests categorical associations, and ANOVA compares multiple groups.
questions.hint: Is the alternative hypothesis directional?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute the range of a dataset
questions.stem: Compute the range of 5, 12, 3, 18, 9.
questions.explanation: The range is max minus min = 18 - 3 = 15. This is a simple measure of spread.
questions.hint: Subtract the smallest value from the largest.

questions.stem: A distribution with a long right tail is:

options.misconception: confuses tail direction with skew label
confuses a tail with symmetry
confuses a tail with flat distribution

questions.explanation: A long right tail means right-skewed (positive skew). Left-skewed has a long left tail, symmetric has no tail, and uniform is flat.
questions.hint: Which direction is the tail pointing?

questions.learningObjective: identify residual pattern indicating poor fit
questions.stem: In a residual plot, a clear curved pattern suggests:

options.misconception: confuses pattern with perfect fit
confuses curvature with constant variance
confuses pattern with absence of outliers

questions.explanation: A curved residual pattern indicates the linear model misses structure in the data. Perfect fit would show no pattern, homoscedasticity concerns spread, and outliers are individual extreme points.
questions.hint: What does structure in residuals reveal about the model?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean means:

options.text: If we repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean
There is a 95% probability the true mean is in this specific interval
options.misconception: confuses frequentist interval with Bayesian posterior

options.text: 95% of the data lies within the interval
options.misconception: confuses confidence interval with data range

options.text: The sample mean equals the true mean 95% of the time
options.misconception: confuses interval coverage with point estimate equality

questions.explanation: Frequentist confidence refers to the long-run coverage of the procedure, not a probability about a fixed parameter. The distractors reflect Bayesian, data-range, and point-estimate misconceptions.
questions.hint: What is random in frequentist inference?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: identify an assumption of linear regression
questions.stem: Which of the following is a standard assumption of ordinary least squares linear regression?

options.text: Residuals are independent and have constant variance
The predictor must be normally distributed
options.misconception: confuses predictor distribution with residual normality
confuses regression with classification

options.text: There must be at least 100 observations
options.misconception: confuses sample size rule of thumb with assumption

questions.explanation: OLS assumes linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, and normality of residuals. The predictor need not be normal, the response is numeric, and sample size is a guideline, not an assumption.
questions.hint: Which assumption concerns the errors, not the predictors?
